criterion_notes.c1: Examines a municipal piped drinking-water conveyance project (Adduction d'eau potable Grombaou) intended to supply drought-affected Kanak villages (Noeli, Tiaoue, and Poindah) as well as complaints over three unserved houses in lower Neami.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the literal plain wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this study would qualify (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') because it examines local municipal water governance and an institutional conflict/negotiation between the elected Municipality Council and the customary Council of Elders within New Caledonia's post-Noumea Agreement decolonization framework. Under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, however, Criterion 2 is 'no': the paper does not study a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements for service connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules governing user access, administrative discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Instead, it analyzes political and indigenous contestation around generic capital-works project delivery/staging (2000-2004 vs. 2005-2009 Development Contracts) and rejected tribal demands for bulk water extraction royalties as a window onto political cleavages within Kanak nationalism (exclude as E03).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative empirical evidence from ethnographic fieldwork in Kone (2002-2004), including participant observation of internal Municipality Council deliberations (7 June 2004) and the tribal-municipal negotiation meeting in Neami (19 July 2004), informal interviews, and text analysis of the 7 June 2004 protest letter.
criterion_notes.c4: Descriptively reports community- and household-level water service availability and connection status within the ethnographic narrative: dry-season water shortages in lower-altitude villages, three unserved houses in lower Neami deferred to the 2005-2009 Development Contract, withdrawal of the pipeline obstruction threat, and inauguration of piped water delivery from Grombaou to Poindah, Tiaoue, and Noeli (although the author's primary analytical focus is political legitimacy rather than water access evaluation).
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (Kanak tribes/villages and municipal/customary actors in the commune of Kone), the qualitative ethnographic case study design, the political-institutional negotiation process, and descriptive village water delivery outcomes, though an eligible rule-type legal/administrative exposure is absent under narrow Criterion 2.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

study_design: Qualitative ethnographic case study (participant observation and document analysis, 2002-2004)
population_and_sample: Kanak tribes/villages (Neami, Noeli, Tiaoue, Poindah) and municipal councillors and customary elders in the commune of Kone, Northern Province, New Caledonia (ethnographic observation of 5 municipal officials on 7 June 2004 and ~20 Neami residents plus 10 municipal staff on 19 July 2004)
exposure: Political-institutional conflict and negotiation between elected municipal authorities and customary tribal elders over municipal water pipeline construction/staging (2000-2004 vs. 2005-2009 Development Contracts) and customary resource royalty demands (not a rule-type mechanism governing service access)
outcome: Withdrawal of pipeline construction blockade threat and inauguration of piped drinking water supply from Grombaou to the tribes of Poindah, Tiaoue, and Noeli (with connection of three unserved houses in lower Neami deferred to the 2005-2009 Development Contract), alongside negotiation of rival electoral vs. customary political legitimacies
rationale: This political anthropology article uses a local dispute over the construction and routing of a municipal drinking-water pipeline (AEP Grombaou) in Kone, New Caledonia, to examine emerging ideological cleavages between pro-independence FLNKS elected officials and customary/'indigenous' Kanak activists. While the ethnography touches on community water supply delivery and passes the literal broad wording of Criterion 2 (institutional/governance conflict between municipal and customary authorities, hence plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'), it fails the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2. The study examines political mobilization around phased public-works infrastructure delivery (2000-2004 vs. 2005-2009 Development Contracts) and rejected tribal demands for bulk resource extraction royalties rather than any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (excluded as E03, Wrong exposure).
